correctness.rationale: Reconstructed the finite proof: a candidate meets each closed neighborhood for domination and each pairwise symmetric difference for separation. These tests are necessary and sufficient. Every subset has one 18-bit mask; at fixed weight every legal adjacency is exactly a swap of one present and one absent bit, independent of their distance in Pappus. Read both frozen programs and their output; the C++ census generates all layers, while the LCF cross-check independently covers all code counts but only the k=9 and k=10 exchange graphs. A separately written program (not a run of the frozen code) checked the incidence/LCF isomorphism, exhausted 262144 subsets, found 52638 codes and none below size nine, and reproduced every code count, edge count and component size in the table. At k=9 it reproduced 1028 vertices, 3780 edges, two 514-vertex components with selected point counts 0–4 and 5–9, and the all-line and all-point centers. BFS from each code gave per-component eccentricities 4:1, 5:27, 6:81, 7:243, 8:162, hence radius four and diameter eight in each component. The incidence graph is self-dual via point (x,y) ↔ line (m=x,b=−y); this also explains the symmetry of the component profiles. Each k=10,…,18 was checked to have exactly one component. value.rationale: An identifying sensor placement must preserve both domination and distinct signatures through each reconfiguration. The unweighted Pappus graph is a natural small symmetric test case in which optimal layouts separate into two geometrically structured regions. Computing the exact next layer and the remaining layers answers the operationally meaningful fixed-size question of how much spare capacity is needed to move between arbitrary valid placements; the answer is exactly one sensor. This conclusion is not just another count of minimum solutions.
residual_risks: No claim that this spare-capacity result generalizes to other cubic graphs or to local sensor moves.
